chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Financial Statements Matter to Managers

lessons.title: Accounting Basics Without the Jargon: Accrual, Revenue Recognition and Ind AS

children.text: On 1 January, CloudSuvidha, a fictional Bengaluru software company, signs a ₹1.2 crore support contract with a Mumbai bank. The full amount is invoiced that week and lands in the bank account on 10 January. The sales head tells his team the year is made.

When the FY25 numbers come out, the P&L shows ₹30 lakh from that contract, not ₹1.2 crore. Nobody has made an error, and nobody is hiding anything. This lesson explains the handful of accounting rules that produce results like this, so the next time finance gives you a number you did not expect, you know why.

body.text: Accounting records events when they economically happen, not when money moves. Almost every confusing number a manager meets comes from that single idea.

children.text: Accrual Accounting: The Rule Behind Everything
There are two ways to keep books.
Cash accounting
records a transaction when money moves.
Accrual accounting
records it when the underlying event happens. Indian companies must use accrual accounting, because Section 128 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires books to be kept on an accrual basis.

markDefs.definition: Recording income when money is received and expenses when money is paid. Simple, but it says nothing about obligations already created.
Recording income when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash moves. Required for company financial statements in India.

body.title: The same year, two sets of books

columns.label: Cash accounting says
points: Expense when you pay the vendor
March electricity bill paid in April belongs to next year
A year of collections can look like a year of performance

columns.label: Accrual accounting says
points: Revenue when you deliver the goods or service
Expense when you consume the benefit
March electricity belongs to March, paid or not
Performance and cash timing are reported separately

children.text: Accrual comes with a partner rule, the matching principle: costs are reported in the same period as the revenue they helped earn. Buy ₹40 lakh of raw material in March and sell the finished goods in June, and the cost sits in inventory until June. It becomes an expense the moment the sale is recorded, not when you paid the supplier.

body.text: This is why "we had a great collection month" and "we had a great month" are different statements. Collections show up in the cash flow statement. Performance shows up in the P&L. Chapter 4 puts the two side by side.

body.title: Which year does the cost belong to?
body.question: On 1 October 2024, your company pays ₹6 lakh for a 12-month insurance policy covering October 2024 to September 2025. The financial year ends on 31 March 2025. How much insurance expense appears in the FY25 P&L?
options: ₹6 lakh, because the full amount was paid in FY25
₹3 lakh, with ₹3 lakh carried forward as a prepaid expense
₹0, because the policy has not expired
body.explanation: Six of the twelve months of cover fall in FY25, so ₹6 lakh × 6 ÷ 12 = ₹3 lakh is the expense. The other ₹3 lakh sits on the balance sheet as a prepaid expense, an asset, and becomes an expense in FY26.

children.text: When Revenue Is Recognised
Revenue is not recognised when you sign the contract, raise the invoice or receive the money. Under
Ind AS 115

, revenue is recognised when control of the goods or services passes to the customer. For a product, that is usually a point in time, on delivery. For a service delivered continuously, such as an annual support contract, it happens over time, month by month.

markDefs.definition: The Indian accounting standard on revenue from contracts with customers, converged with IFRS 15. It replaced the older revenue standards and introduced a single five-step model.

body.latex: \text{Revenue for the period} = \text{Contract value} \times \frac{\text{Months of service delivered}}{\text{Total months in the contract}}
body.caption: The simplest over-time case: an even service contract

children.text: Back to CloudSuvidha. The contract runs from 1 January to 31 December 2025. By 31 March 2025, the company has delivered three of the twelve months.

body.caption: CloudSuvidha: a ₹1.2 crore annual contract across two financial years

cells: Deferred revenue on the balance sheet at year end

stats.label: Deferred revenue
stats.context: A liability: service still owed to the customer

children.text: Deferred revenue

is money you have taken but not yet earned. Until CloudSuvidha delivers those nine months of support, it owes the bank a service, and that obligation is a liability. This is why subscription and annual maintenance businesses can be flush with cash and still report modest revenue.

markDefs.definition: Cash collected from a customer before the goods or services have been delivered. Also called a contract liability, it sits on the balance sheet until the company performs.

body.title: Your turn: two months of service
body.prompt: CloudSuvidha signs a second contract worth ₹96 lakh on 1 February 2025, covering 12 months of support from that date, invoiced and collected upfront. How much revenue from this contract appears in FY25, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: February and March fall in FY25, so ₹96 lakh × 2 ÷ 12 = ₹16 lakh. The remaining ₹80 lakh is deferred revenue on 31 March 2025 and is recognised through FY26.

body.title: The five steps behind Ind AS 115

children.text: Finance teams work through these five steps for any significant contract. You do not have to apply them, but knowing them explains most revenue questions you will ever ask.
Identify the contract
with the customer, including agreed payment terms.
Identify the performance obligations
, the distinct promises in it. A contract for software plus two years of support contains two.
Determine the transaction price
, including discounts, rebates, penalties and variable fees.
Allocate the price
across the performance obligations, based on what each would sell for on its own.
Recognise revenue
as each obligation is satisfied, at a point in time or over time.

Step 2 is where managers get surprised. Bundle free installation and a year of service into a product price, and finance will split that single price across all three promises and spread part of it over the year.

body.title: The 30 March invoice
body.scenario: It is 28 March. Your regional sales target is short by ₹80 lakh. A distributor agrees to be invoiced now for stock that will actually be shipped in the third week of May, with an informal understanding that payment can wait and unsold stock can come back. Your sales manager asks finance to raise the invoice before 31 March.
body.prompt: What is wrong with this, and what would you do instead?
body.modelAnswer:
What is wrong:
1. Revenue is recognised when control passes to the customer, not when an invoice is raised. Goods still in your warehouse in March have not transferred control, so this is not FY25 revenue.
2. A right to return unsold stock means the sale is not final. Even after shipment, revenue would be limited to what is not expected to come back.
3. Auditors test exactly this at year end through cut-off procedures, matching dispatch documents and gate registers against invoice dates. This is one of the most commonly detected manipulations in Indian audits.
4. Recording it anyway overstates FY25 revenue and receivables, and next year opens with a hole plus a returns problem. This is channel stuffing, and it has ended careers.
What to do instead:
5. Report the shortfall honestly, with the May order as visible pipeline for FY26.
6. If you want genuine March revenue, sell something that can actually be delivered in March, for example advancing a delivery the customer already wants.
7. Ask finance to confirm treatment in writing before committing to anything unusual. If it needs an informal side understanding to work, it does not work.

children.text: The Accrual Entries a Manager Meets
Six adjustments cover nearly everything that makes a number look odd to a non-finance manager. Learn these and most of the mystery goes away.

body.caption: Six common accruals, in plain language

cells: A cost incurred but not yet billed or paid
March electricity of ₹4 lakh, billed in April: expense in FY25, liability on 31 March
Cash paid in advance for a benefit not yet consumed
₹6 lakh annual insurance paid on 1 October: ₹3 lakh expense, ₹3 lakh asset
Cash collected before the service is delivered
An estimated obligation that is probable but not yet exact
Performance bonus for the year, decided in April but earned through the year
The cost of a long-lived asset spread over its useful life
A ₹50 lakh packing machine over 10 years: ₹5 lakh a year, no cash outflow
Treating spending as an asset rather than an expense
That ₹50 lakh machine hits the balance sheet, not the P&L, on the day it is bought

body.text: Provisions and estimates are where judgement enters the accounts. How much of your receivables will go bad, how long a machine will last, what the warranty claims will be. These are honest estimates, not facts, and two reasonable finance teams can land on different numbers. Chapter 6 shows how to spot when estimates are being stretched.

body.title: Name the liability
body.textWithBlank: Cash collected from a customer before the service has been delivered is shown on the balance sheet as ___ revenue.
body.explanation: Deferred revenue, also called a contract liability or unearned revenue, is an obligation to deliver, not income. It becomes revenue only as the company performs.

children.text: Ind AS: Which Rulebook Your Company Follows
Indian companies do not all use the same rulebook. Which one applies decides how your numbers look.
Ind AS

, the Indian Accounting Standards converged with global IFRS, apply to all companies listed on NSE or BSE other than those on the SME platform, and to unlisted companies with a net worth of ₹250 crore or more. They were phased in from 2016-17.
AS
, the older Accounting Standards, continue for smaller unlisted companies.
The practical difference for a manager is that Ind AS leans towards showing economic reality, even when that makes the balance sheet larger or profits more volatile. The clearest example is leases.

body.label: Ind AS 116, effective 1 April 2019
body.value: Your office lease is now an asset and a liability
body.context: Rented offices and warehouses used to be an off balance sheet rent expense. Under Ind AS 116, a lessee records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for most leases, so rent is replaced by depreciation plus interest. Companies with large rented footprints, such as retail chains, saw their balance sheets grow substantially with no change in the underlying business.

children.text: Three assumptions sit under all of it. The company is a going concern, expected to continue operating. The books are kept on an accrual basis. Policies are applied consistently year to year, so that this year can be compared with last year.

body.label: MCA: Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)
body.description: The official text of the notified standards. Useful when you need to check what a standard actually says rather than what a blog claims it says.

body.title: Translate your own department
steps: Name one cost your team incurs in a month but pays for later. That is an accrued expense.
Name one payment your team makes upfront for a year of benefit. That is a prepaid expense.
If your company sells contracts or subscriptions, ask finance how much deferred revenue sits on the balance sheet.
Find one asset your team uses daily and ask over how many years it is depreciated.
Check whether your employer reports under Ind AS or AS. If it is listed on NSE or BSE and not on the SME platform, it is Ind AS.
Ask your finance business partner which estimate in their accounts involves the most judgement.

cards.definition: Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, whatever the cash timing. Required under Section 128 of the Companies Act, 2013.
Reporting costs in the same period as the revenue they helped generate.
Recording revenue when control of goods or services passes to the customer, at a point in time or over time.
Cash collected before delivery. A liability until the company performs.
Cash paid before the benefit is consumed. An asset until it is used up.
An estimated obligation that is probable but not yet precisely known, such as a bonus or warranty cost.
Indian Accounting Standards converged with IFRS, applicable to listed companies other than SME platform companies and to unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250 crore or more.
The assumption that the company will keep operating for the foreseeable future, which is why assets are not valued at fire sale prices.

points: Indian company accounts are kept on an accrual basis: events are recorded when they happen, not when cash moves.
The matching principle puts costs in the same period as the revenue they helped earn.
Revenue is recognised when control passes to the customer, which can be on delivery or spread across a service period.
Cash collected in advance is deferred revenue, a liability, not income.
Accrued expenses, prepaid expenses, provisions, depreciation and capitalisation explain most numbers that surprise managers.
Listed companies other than those on the SME platform, and unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250 crore or more, report under Ind AS, which puts leases on the balance sheet.

body.text: CloudSuvidha is fictional and the figures are simplified for teaching. Accounting standards and their applicability thresholds are amended from time to time, so confirm the current position with your finance team or auditor before relying on it for a decision.
